Furthermore "... In Ashraf Ali Vs. State (Delhi) 1991 SCC 203, it has been observed that: "The testimony of a witness is not to be disbelieved or discarded on the ground that the he happens to be an official witness but it is an equally well recognized rule of caution that Court should look for independent corroboration to the testimony of official witness in such cases.
Relevant, of course, in the context are the time and opportunity available to the police party to associate with such an independent witness.
It is a matter of common knowledge that no public person would like to involve himself by becoming a witness of recovery.

Minor contradictions are bound to occur if a witness is examined after a considerable time..."

In the case in hand, all prosecution witnesses have clearly deposed that despite efforts none from the public had agreed to join as a witness.
Thus this argument of the accused does not hold much weight.
24. Another leg of argument of Ld. Counsel for accused is that price of the sample paid, was less then what is mentioned on Ex.PW1/A1.
However, Ld. Counsel for the accused has failed to make note of the fact that the said pamphlet Ex.PW1/A1 itself mentions that the prices are subject to increase or decrease as per market rate.
The pamphlet Ex.PW1/A1 also does not bear any date which can show that on the date of lifting the sample i.e. 20.06.2009 the price of 'ghee' was Rs.200/- Kg.
Hence the submission of the Ld.
Counsel for the accused is not tenable.

Perusal of the record reveals that PA report dated 06.07.2009 was sent to the accused by post on 26.11.2009.
Complainant has placed on record Ex.PW1/K and Ex.PW1/L in support of its case.
Further PW-1 in his testimony has deposed that the report sent by post was not received back.
It is also not the case of the accused that copy of Ex.PW1/G was not received by him.

Further the relevant provisions under which the copy of PA report is required to be sent to the accused are as under:
Section 13 Report of public analyst-(2) On receipt of the report of the result of the analysis under sub-section (1) to the effect that the article of food is adulterated, the Local (Health) Authority shall, after the institution of prosecution against the persons from whom the sample of the article of food was taken and the person, if any, whose name, address and other particulars have been disclosed under section 14A, forward,
in such manner as may be prescribed, a copy of the report of the result of the analysis to such person or persons, as the case may be, informing such person or persons that if it is so desired, either or both of them may make an application to the court within a period of ten days from the date of receipt of the copy of the report to get the sample of the article of food kept by the Local (Health) Authority analysed by the Central Food Laboratory"

Further as per Rule 9B, the LHA shall within a period of 10 days after the initiation of prosecution forward a copy of the report of the result by registered post or by hand to the person from whom the sample of the article was taken.

28. Thus, it can be seen that Sub-section (2) of Section 13 of the Act confers valuable right on the accused under which provision, the accused can make an application to the court within a period of 10 days from the receipt of copy of the report of Public Analyst to get the samples of food analysed in the Central Food Laboratory.

However as observed by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in "T.V Usman v. Food Inspector, Tellicherry" (AIR 1994 SC 1818) that mere delay as such will not per se be fatal to the prosecution case even in cases where the sample continues to remain fit for analysis inspite of the delay because the accused is in no way prejudiced on the merits of the case in respect of such delay.

30. It is to be considered that the sample article in the present case is 'ghee' which has long shelf life and delay of about five to six months would not have resulted the sample becoming unfit for examination.
Also the sample as such was found to be sub- standard due to high B.R Reading and low R.M Value which indicates that the 'ghee' could be adulterated with vegetable oil or animal body fat.
Also as per Ex.PW1/G the Baudouin test was found to be positive.
The test, as such indicates presence of Vanaspati hydrogenated fat, refined vegetable oil or animal fats in ghee.
Thus, delay of few months in sending the sample article to RFL would not have hampered the right of the accused with respect to above findings.

31. As regards the second allegation by the complainant against the accused not disclosing the name of the person from whom the food article was purchased, the same is also mentioned at serial no. 15 of Ex.PW1/D1 and no evidence has been led by the accused to rebut the same.

32. On bare reading of Section 7 of the Act, it is clear that the liability under the Act is absolute i.e.
there is total elimination of mens era.
So the liability of a person contravening any of the provision contained in Section 7 is an absolute liability and it does not depend upon the existence of any particular knowledge or intention.

34. In P. K. Tejani v. M. r. Dange, (1974) CrLJ 313 (SC), Hon'ble Justice Krishna Iyer observed that,
in food offences strict liability is the rule not merely under IPC but all over the world.

In this Act unless the context otherwise requires, ia)
"adulterated"-an article of food shall be deemed to be adulterated:-
(a) if the article sold by a vendor is not of the nature, substance or quality demanded by the purchaser and is to his prejudice, or is not of the nature, substance or quality which it purports or is represented to be;
(b) if the article contains any other substance which affects, or if the article is so processed as to affect, injuriously the nature, substance or quality thereof;
(c) if any inferior or cheaper substance has been substituted wholly or in part for the article so as to affect injuriously the nature,substance or quality thereof;
(m) if the quality or purity of the article falls below the prescribed standard or its constituents are present in quantities not within the prescribed limits of variability but which does not render it injurious to health;

Further the relevant provisions under which the copy of PA report is required to be sent to the accused are as under:
Section 13 Report of public analyst-(2) On receipt of the report of the result of the analysis under sub-section (1) to the effect that the article of food is adulterated, the Local (Health) Authority shall, after the institution of prosecution against the persons from whom the sample of the article of food was taken and the person, if any, whose name, address and other particulars have been disclosed under section 14A, forward,
in such manner as may be prescribed, a copy of the report of the result of the analysis to such person or persons, as the case may be, informing such person or persons that if it is so desired, either or both of them may make an application to the court within a period of ten days from the date of receipt of the copy of the report to get the sample of the article of food kept by the Local (Health) Authority analysed by the Central Food Laboratory"
NABEELA WALI WALI Date: 2022.10.17 17:11:58 +0530 CC No:- 42902/2016 DA (FSO) v. Ravi Kumar Etc.
28. Thus, it can be seen that Sub-section (2) of Section 13 of the Act confers valuable right on the accused under which provision, the accused can make an application to the court within a period of 10 days from the receipt of copy of the report of Public Analyst to get the samples of food analysed in the Central Food Laboratory.
However as observed by Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in "T.V Usman v. Food Inspector, Tellicherry" (AIR 1994 SC 1818) that mere delay as such will not per se be fatal to the prosecution case even in cases where the sample continues to remain fit for analysis inspite of the delay because the accused is in no way prejudiced on the merits of the case in respect of such delay.
Therefore it must be shown that the delay has led to the denial of right conferred under Section 13(2) and that depends on the facts of each case and violation of the time limit can not be a ground for the prosecution case being thrown out.
29. In the present case, the complaint was filed on 23.11.2009 and the report Ex.PW1/G was sent to the accused by post on NABEELA WALI WALI Date:
2022.10.17 17:12:06 +0530 CC No:- 42902/2016 DA (FSO) v. Ravi Kumar Etc.
Nothing has been put on record by the accused to show non-compliance of Rule 9B of the PFA Rules.
Thereafter the accused was required to make an application before this court within a period of ten days from the date of receipt of the copy of the report.
Furthermore in view of the observation of Hon'ble Apex Court in "T.V Usman v. Food Inspector, Tellicherry" (AIR 1994 SC 1818) the accused was required to show that the delay resulted in the sample becoming unfit for examination.
Also the sample as such was found to be sub- standard due to high B.R Reading and low R.M Value which indicates that the 'ghee' could be adulterated with vegetable oil or animal body fat.
Also as per Ex.PW1/G the Baudouin test was found to be positive.
The test, as such indicates presence of Vanaspati hydrogenated fat, refined vegetable oil or animal fats in ghee.
Thus, delay of few months in sending the sample article to RFL would not have hampered the right of the accused with respect to above findings.
Hence this argument by by NABEELA NABEELA WALI WALI Date:
2022.10.17 17:12:14 +0530 CC No:- 42902/2016 DA (FSO) v. Ravi Kumar Etc.
32. On bare reading of Section 7 of the Act, it is clear that the liability under the Act is absolute i.e.
there is total elimination of mens era.
So the liability of a person contravening any of the provision contained in Section 7 is an absolute liability and it does not depend upon the existence of any particular knowledge or intention.
